summary:
Terengganu is one of the 13 states of Malaysia and stands under the national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years plus whipping. Sodomy has been criminalised in Malaysian law since 1871, and these sections are not limited to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor in Terengganu is exposed to them on the same terms as a resident.

The state layer adds a second offence that reaches only Muslims. All 13 states, Terengganu included, maintain Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Enforcement sits with the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact.

Official messaging from the Terengganu state government is openly hostile. In May 2025 a state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices installed at strategic locations across the state are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, stating that the state wants people to regard those acts as "dirty, wrong, and to be avoided".

Thirteen civil-society organisations, among them Justice for Sisters, responded the same month by urging the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove the signboards. They condemned the boards as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law, and criticised the executive councillor's defence of them as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBT people.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, while the Penal Code provisions do. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Terengganu's official campaign sits inside a national enforcement pattern in which raids produce large-scale arrests and public exposure. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media had been pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid, and police raided another sauna in Penang days later.

Religious enforcement also targets visible trans figures. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked.

Trans women in Malaysia have been killed with documented official indifference. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

Comparative movement is limited to the state layer: the Federal Court's federalism rulings in Selangor and Kelantan removed cross-dressing provisions there, while the federal Penal Code provisions survived every challenge intact.
localsOnly:
Residents who are Muslim in Terengganu fall under the state Sharia enactment on cross-dressing, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, enforced by the state Islamic religious department. Because the enactments define no test for what counts as transgender dressing, the offence turns on the assessing officer's judgement rather than on a stated standard.

The signboard programme is directed at the state's own population. The executive councillor's May 2025 statement frames the boards as a deliberate instrument for producing aversion, and the counter-campaign by 13 organisations, including Justice for Sisters, was addressed to the Kuala Terengganu City Council as the body responsible for the installations.

Legal protection for LGBT residents is thin across Malaysia. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law, and constitutional challenges to the Sharia cross-dressing offences have failed at the High Court. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects.
